title: AI Encounters of the Dubious Kind: Bjork, generative learning and the need to think for yourself.
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington examines pedagogical risks of unguarded AI adoption in schools, using ChatGPT hallucinations as a concrete example. His central concern is that LLM confidence in false outputs, combined with student vulnerability to automation bias, creates dual dangers: students accept confident misinformation without critical evaluation; delegating thinking tasks to AI atrophies independent reasoning through a "delegation feedback loop." Sherrington synthesizes research on cognitive offloading, noting high AI use correlates with weaker critical thinking, reduced memory, narrower problem-solving, and diminished curiosity. He advocates embedding AI within generative learning frameworks where students engage in deep thinking, self-explanation, peer teaching, and self-testing—using AI to prompt rather than replace cognitive work.
points: Confidence in falsehood is signature risk: ChatGPT confuses singer Bjork with cognitive science principle, invents reasoning.
Cognitive offloading correlates with measurable decline: higher AI dependence predicts lower reasoning, weakened critical thinking, diminished memory.
Automation bias and reduced critical evaluation pose long-term risks; students lose habit of checking, challenging information.
Generative learning must remain central; AI can prompt self-explanation, peer teaching, accuracy-checking—not replace intellectual work.
Safeguards for AI in education are weak; teachers must design tasks demanding authentic student thinking.
quotes: The confidence projected in the response is alarming—given how wrong it is.
If I was a student novice doing a search I might not notice at all.
AI massively accelerates cognitive offloading. Instead of thinking through a problem, users jump straight to an answer.
People using AI heavily tend to think less deeply.
